results.summary: This is a single two-input OR gate implemented in Verilog on a one-tile design. Inputs A and B are on ui[0] and ui[1], and the OR result appears on uo[0]. It is tested by applying all four input combinations and observing the output. The documentation describes it as a simple test of the Verilog chip creation flow, so it is essentially a beginner template with no external hardware required.

TinyQV is a small RV32EC Risc-V SoC with Zcb and Zicond extensions, using 28-bit addresses and 24-bit program addresses, with instructions fetched over QSPI from flash and data stored in QSPI PSRAM. The flash and RAM share QSPI clock and data lines, so only one can be accessed at a time, and code can only execute from flash. It is used with a QSPI PMOD containing 16MB flash and two 8MB RAMs, and its UART pins match the RP2040 hardware UART on the demo board; reset and flash programming are handled by MicroPython scripts. The design is an early version of the Tiny Tapeout crowdsourced Risc-V challenge, with peripherals contributed by the community and a documented maximum QSPI read latency of 3 cycles.

This is a 4-bit adder that takes two 4-bit numbers on ui[0:3] and ui[4:7] and produces a 5-bit sum on uo[0:4]. It is tested by connecting buttons or DIP switches to the eight inputs and LEDs to the five outputs. The design is a straightforward Wokwi beginner project with no on-chip peripherals. The documentation is minimal but sufficient to describe the function and required external hardware.

DigOTA is described as a digital implementation of an operational transconductance amplifier that requires a 50 kHz clock and two input signals, producing three outputs. The output current is said to be proportional to the number of pulses in the output stages, suggesting a pulse-density or switched scheme rather than a true analog OTA. The documentation does not specify the input or output voltage/current ranges, nor any external components needed. It is a Wokwi design with very thin documentation, so most operational details cannot be verified.

This is a 4-bit incrementer that takes a 4-bit input on ui[0:3] and produces a 5-bit output on uo[0:4], presumably the input plus one. The documentation says only to test it, without describing expected values or a test procedure. It requires VCC as external hardware according to the project notes. The design is a minimal Wokwi exercise with almost no useful documentation.

This project contains a collection of logic gates with eight inputs and eight outputs, intended as a Wokwi workshop exercise. It is tested by checking truth tables for the implemented gates. No external hardware is required. The documentation is very sparse and does not identify which gates are present or how inputs map to outputs.

This project is explicitly titled "in progress" and its description says only that it "does something." The test instructions and external hardware sections are placeholders that promise details later. No function, interface, or implementation is described, so nothing concrete can be said about the design. It appears to be an unfinished Wokwi template.

The project claims to model a chip design and to let the user view a 3D model of it. It has eight inputs and three outputs, but the documentation does not explain what the design computes or how the pins are used. No external hardware is specified beyond a placeholder line. The description is too vague to determine the actual function, and it reads like an unfinished Wokwi exercise.

This is described as an 8-to-3 encoder with eight inputs and three outputs, which matches a standard priority or binary encoder function. The how-it-works and how-to-test sections are placeholders saying only that something needs to be changed. No external hardware is listed. The documentation is essentially absent, so the exact encoding behavior cannot be confirmed.

This project is a first attempt at using Wokwi, described as an experiment feeding inputs to an LED number display. The test instructions explicitly say not to use it because it is not good. External hardware is listed only as "yes" with no detail. The documentation is too thin to determine the actual circuit or behavior.
